Sith
SITH
conjunction
From Old English sithþan (“after that, since”), the older, fuller form that contracted into the modern “since”; meaning “seeing that,” “inasmuch as,” or “because.”

Biblical Definition

Sith is the elder form of “since,” carrying both its senses — “from the time that” and, as here, the causal “seeing that, because.” It stands once in the KJV, in the oracle against Mount Seir: “I will prepare thee unto blood, and blood shall pursue thee: sith thou hast not hated blood, even blood shall pursue thee” (Eze 35:6). The word is the fulcrum of a fearful justice. Because Edom did not hate the shedding of blood — loved it, rather, and shed his brother Israel’s in the day of calamity (Eze 35:5) — blood is appointed to hunt him down. The sin names the sentence: the man who will not hate blood shall be pursued by it. Here is the ancient law written large: “Whoso sheddeth man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed” (Gen 9:6), for man bears the image of God, and violence against the image is answered in kind. Our Lord seals the same principle: “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52). The little “sith” binds crime to consequence with an iron logic — not arbitrary wrath, but the moral order of a God who requires the blood of the innocent. Edom’s doom hangs on that hinge, and so does every unrepented cruelty; the God who says “sith thou hast not hated blood” still governs a world where sin summons its own pursuer.

Webster 1828 Definition

The old, fuller form of “since,” meaning “seeing that” or “because” — the hinge of judgment on bloodguilty Edom.

SITH, since; seeing that; inasmuch as; because.

From Old English sithþan, “after that,” the elder form of “since.”

It stands once in the KJV: “sith thou hast not hated blood” (Eze 35:6).

It binds Edom’s crime to its sentence: blood shall pursue the lover of blood.

The causal “sith” names the sin that names the doom.

Key Scripture

Eze 35:6 — "Therefore, as I live, saith the Lord GOD, I will prepare thee unto blood, and blood shall pursue thee: sith thou hast not hated blood, even blood shall pursue thee."

Eze 35:5 — "Because thou hast had a perpetual hatred, and hast shed the blood of the children of Israel by the force of the sword in the time of their calamity, in the time that their iniquity had an end:"

Gen 9:6 — "Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man."

Mat 26:52 — "Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword."

Modern Corruption

Not a contested doctrine but an obsolete conjunction; it recovers the causal logic of divine justice — the sin that summons its own sentence.

expand to see more

The word rebukes the age’s severing of deed from consequence. “Sith thou hast not hated blood” ties Edom’s doom straight to Edom’s cruelty; the sentence is not arbitrary but earned. A generation that will not hate the shedding of innocent blood — that shrugs at violence, at the destruction of the image of God in the weak and unborn — stands under the same causal “sith.” Sin is never idle; it summons its own pursuer, and blood cries from the ground (Gen 4:10).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the moral coherence of God’s judgments: He gives reasons, and the reason is our sin. “Sith” is the hinge that keeps justice from looking like caprice — the LORD says why. Against this stands the only refuge, the blood that speaketh better things than that of Abel (Heb 12:24), which pleads not vengeance but mercy for all who hate their sin and flee to Christ.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The elder form of “since,” “sith” means “because” — the causal hinge fastening Edom’s cruelty to Edom’s doom.

Sith — Old English sithþan, “after that”; elder form of “since.”

It means “seeing that,” “inasmuch as,” “because.”
